claims: T1 frame: the causes of the war in Europe and the factors behind Germany's eventual collapse ('roke' / defeat), divided into the outbreak and the reasons for defeat
T2 Treaty of Versailles (1919): harsh terms, massive reparations, severe military cutbacks, territorial losses; deep national resentment and a desire for revision
T3 economic instability: the Great Depression of 1929 shattered the German economy, causing massive unemployment and hyperinflation, destabilizing the Weimar Republic
T4 Nazi ideology and Lebensraum: Hitler and the Nazi Party promised to restore pride, overturn Versailles and conquer Lebensraum in Eastern Europe for the Aryan race
T5 appeasement: Britain and France's concessions (parts of Czechoslovakia) emboldened Hitler's aggression
T6 the invasion of Poland, September 1, 1939, prompting Britain and France to declare war
T7 defeat: overextended supply lines across the Soviet Union; shortages of fuel, food and warm clothing (the halt before Moscow, 1941)
T8 two-front war split the Wehrmacht's forces and industrial output
T9 economic and industrial disparity: the US (Lend-Lease), Soviet human and material resources and the British Empire far outproduced the German war economy
T10 catastrophic setbacks: Stalingrad (1943) and the failed offensive at Kursk halted expansion and forced a permanent retreat
T11 Allied air superiority: round-the-clock strategic bombing devastated cities, infrastructure, industrial production and civilian morale
T12 offer: the Ruhr Pocket (1945), if a specific event was meant

sentences.text: Germany's role in the Second World War was that of a war state bent on conquest: on achieving power Hitler smashed the nation's democratic institutions and made Germany a war state intent on conquering Europe for the benefit of the so-called Aryan race, and his invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939 triggered the European phase of the war (National WWII Museum); that state, #1669 argues, was an advanced industrial power for which labor became a binding wartime constraint, and its land program, Lebensraum, modeled on the American and British empires, was turned in practice into a labor supply.

The causes, the Holocaust Explained schools site writes, are neither singular nor straightforward: Germany's aggressive foreign policy was not the sole cause but 'a large contributing factor', decisive in the outbreak, while the failure or inability of other countries to react was also key; History.com finds the war caused in part by the Great Depression and by political tensions left unresolved after the First World War; History Hit calls Hitler's rise and his determination to build a dominating Third Reich the ultimate cause, though not the only one; and two German embassies' posts, by their titles, place the causes in the ideology of National Socialism and state that Germany was responsible for the outbreak.

Versailles, which the Allies compelled the Weimar Republic to accept with $33 billion in reparations, a radically downsized army and a ban on submarines and an air force, outraged and humiliated Hitler and other patriotic Germans (National WWII Museum); History Hit calls its terms, set at French insistence, punitive in the extreme, leaving Germany destitute and its people feeling victimised; paying the reparations brought runaway inflation, four billion marks to the dollar by September 1923 (National WWII Museum), and History.com holds that Weimar's political and economic instability and lingering resentment over Versailles fueled the rise of Hitler and his party.

The worldwide depression and the rising power of unions and communists turned growing numbers of Germans to the Nazi Party, which fed on bank failures and unemployment, and the party went from 2.6 percent of the vote in 1928 to the largest party in the Reichstag by 1932, Hindenburg appointing Hitler chancellor the following January (National WWII Museum); the Wall Street Crash of 1929 turned economic into political instability and support for extremists (Holocaust Explained), the Depression creating conditions such as widespread unemployment that facilitated the party's rise (History Hit); and Hitler, though führer with supreme authority, could not have risen or committed the atrocities alone, having the active support of the officer class and of millions of citizens who voted for the party (National WWII Museum).

Hitler expanded the army, reintroduced conscription and began a new air force, all violations of Versailles (National WWII Museum); from 1935 Germany pursued an aggressive foreign policy, planning for war in the Hossbach Memorandum of 1937 and occupying Austria, the Sudetenland and Czechoslovakia before invading Poland (Holocaust Explained), and it rearmed without sanction or protest from Britain or France (History Hit); for Evans the war economy was in place before 1939, with a clampdown on consumers and massive borrowing for arms, and Blitzkrieg as a conscious strategy is a myth; #1669 sets Germany's entry into the Nazi period as an advanced industrial power, quoting Rüdiger Hachtmann on the Fordist production regime gaining ground 'in ever broader sectors of industry' from 1936 at the latest; Hachtmann applies the term 'war Fordism' to the years from 1933, and writes that with full employment from 1934–35 forms of work organization that promised to replace qualified workers with unqualified ones became increasingly attractive.

Hoping to avoid war, Britain and France chose appeasement over Czechoslovakia (National WWII Museum); Hitler counted on the reluctance of Britain and Europe to intervene, for fear of another war (USHMM), and appeasement boosted his confidence and made his actions bolder (Holocaust Explained); the Nazi-Soviet pact carved up the buffer zone between the two powers and paved the way for the invasion of Poland (History Hit), spared Hitler a war on two fronts there, France and Britain declaring war two days after the invasion (History.com), and let the Nazis start the war for Lebensraum with Soviet support (Holocaust Explained).

The party's ultimate aim, in the National WWII Museum's account, was power, a dictatorship and a racially pure community led in a campaign of racial cleansing and world conquest; Hitler believed war the only way to gain Lebensraum for the race he called Aryan (History.com), and in May 1939 bound the coming war to Lebensraum in the East, Central Europe and Russia up to the Volga (History Hit); #1669 reports the field's reading of the East as a war for land and empire, Adam Tooze calling it 'the last great land grab in the long and bloody history of European colonialism', gives the East also as an answer to blockade from the English Table Talk of September 1941, a text #1669 grades weak and to be checked against the German editions, and reports Robert Gordon's objection that the Nazis 'failed to see the obvious solution', to move labor out of agriculture, on which reading Lebensraum was the wrong answer.

A conquered Soviet Union was to be ruled by the German master race, which would exterminate or subdue millions of Slavs for Lebensraum, with model farms and factories (National WWII Museum); Evans gives Hitler's aims as the conquest and racial reordering of Eastern Europe into a European version of the American West, Germans as settlers and the indigenous population enslaved and eventually eliminated, and the General Plan for the East, drafted in 1941–2, as envisaging 30 to 45 million Slavs perishing through starvation and disease or worked to death, with German settlers replacing them; the planners, #1669 states, described the East in the vocabulary of overseas empire and the American West, USHMM writing that Hitler and other Nazi thinkers 'drew direct comparisons to American expansion in the West'.

The German term for the practice, inner colonization, 'an ethnically based settler colonialism' in Robert Nelson's words, was older than Nazism, and its continuity runs through an institution and its personnel, Himmler's RKF and Konrad Meyer, who penned the first iteration of General Plan East, a plan 'calling for the emptying of the eastern space, followed by its filling with German settlers', while the founder of the doctrine stands outside the deportations (#1669); Eastern Europe, in Willeke Sandler's words, 'offered readily accessible territory for the fulfillment of colonial ambitions', the East as colonial empire is, by #1669's report of the field, the least contested part of the colonial reading of Nazism, and the colonial relation, #1669 holds, was relocated from overseas to the continent.

Continuity from German South West Africa is contested: Jürgen Zimmerer, as Mohamed Adhikari reports, points 'especially to continuities with the horrors perpetrated by the Nazi regime four decades later', Alan Kramer finds it 'problematic to see the colonial camps as antecedents in a genealogical line at the end of which stand the Nazi death camps', and Adhikari holds that 'an explanation of Nazi violence cannot simply be reduced to colonial influences'; #1669 takes Kramer's word, setting concentration, forced labor by captives, racial classification and settler clearance in a common archive from about 1900, claims no line of descent from Windhoek to the Nazi camps, and places the joining of the camp to the assembly line in 1942–44 and in German industry.

Lebensraum answered with land, and what conquest delivered to the factory, from 1940 onward, was people (#1669): with male workers drafted to the front and women not further mobilized there were 8 million foreign, mostly forced labourers in Germany by mid-1944 (Evans), and after the armistice 650,000 Italian soldiers were shipped to Germany as forced labourers to join millions drafted from Poland and the Soviet Union in place of German workers sent to the front (Evans, writing in The Guardian, where he is given as regius professor of modern history at Cambridge); #1669 reports Ulrich Herbert's more than eight million foreign forced laborers in the war economy in 1944 and his judgment that without foreign labor German agricultural and industrial production 'would have collapsed in 1942 at the latest', USHMM's more than 7,500,000 non-German workers registered in the Reich in August 1944, Herbert's 7.6 million, 5.7 million civilians and a little under 2 million prisoners of war, and his typical forced laborer of 1943, 'an eighteen-year-old school girl from Kiev', and it notes that the figures differ by denominator, the stock on a date or the flow across the war, the Reich alone or the occupied territories with it.

Conquest became labor policy, #1669 argues, a chain from military occupation through recruitment and deportation to registration in the Reich, segregated barracks and the plant: by Hachtmann's dating the labour force was recruited, 'above all from 1941 onward, as a kind of war booty' from occupied Europe and no longer protected by the usual labour laws, recruitment ran along Mark Spoerer's gradient of force from pure advertising to deportation by arbitrary violence, territory and labor moved in opposite directions, and Herbert reads the enforced foreign labor program as foreshadowing 'a hierarchical National Socialist society founded on racial criteria' across the conquered continent; the colonial seizure of the East and the staffing of German industry became, on #1669's reading, interlocking operations of the same conquest regime.

Hannah Arendt's continental imperialism, as #1669 quotes her, has a 'concept of cohesive expansion' that 'does not allow for any geographic distance between the methods and institutions of colony and of nation': 'Continental imperialism truly begins at home'; on #1669's reading the colony entered the factory and conquest was metabolized at the industrial core, while Arendt did not carry her own frame into the labor relation, having judged the camps economically irrelevant, a judgment #1669 cites through Wikipedia and has yet to locate in her text.

War Fordism is Hachtmann's term for the form in which Fordism, workplace rationalization and especially assembly-line production, but also a 'technology of domination' and an 'exploitation innovation', was established in broad sectors of German industry under Nazi rule (#1669); #1669 reads it as decomposing work horizontally, one process become a row of operations, each specified, timed and assigned to a station, a job that whoever can perform one operation can staff, the worker supplied after 1941 by conquest; the production form preceded the camp labor that entered it, camp prisoners entering regular industrial mass production from August 1942 at the Heinkel plant in Oranienburg, and by Hachtmann's verdict prisoner deployment 'delayed the leap to (partial) automation' and the connection of Fordism and extreme forced labour 'led to a dead end'.

The racial state, #1669 holds, decomposed persons vertically, and on one line the two cuts crossed: Herbert names the contradiction between the economic interest in exploiting as many foreigners as possible and the ideological principle of protecting the Volk from 'foreign blood', from which 'a rigidly hierarchical racist system for the treatment of forced laborers' developed; Spoerer ranks 'Nordic' peoples at the top and Jews and Sinti and Roma at the bottom and calls the regime for Poles and Ostarbeiter 'apartheid'; by Hachtmann's account foreign labourers, eastern labourers above all, formed the core of the Fordist rationalization proletariat from 1941, while male German workers who remained in the plants advanced to become racially privileged foremen and head workmen; deprivation and death, in Peter Hayes's words, 'were not equally distributed'; and industrial modernity, #1669 concludes, kept radically unfree labor and learned to compose standardized production with graded human status.

Read in the grammar of the argument's first half, which followed the laboring body from noun to verb, from the priced person of the plantation ledger to the timed operation of the Ford line (#1668, as #1669 states it), slavery priced the noun, Fordism specified the verb, and war Fordism kept the specified verb and made the noun a switch: a racial-juridical classification assigned by the state to whole populations taken in conquest selected the coercive regime under which the verb was extracted, so that the same general act, reading productive capacity, had radically different consequences depending on juridical-racial status (#1669); the SS, USHMM states, killed those it judged unable to work, often within two or three hours of arrival, and used those who could work for forced labor, putting them to death when they could no longer work, and, in USHMM's words that #1669 quotes, 'the ability to work offered the chance of survival to Jews, for those deemed unable to work were the first to be shot or deported'.

Hachtmann's aptitude tests cross the grade: almost 500,000 civilian foreign labourers in more than 1,000 companies were examined, and from the autumn of 1943 camp prisoners irrespective of their national ('racial') affiliation, testing that 'tended to undermine the racist schema' and 'says little about the core issue'; the racial classification, #1669 holds, came from the state, the production system's own measures tended to disregard it, and the state installed it anyway, while within the range it set measured capacity, firm, workplace, sex, date and local administration also mattered.

The camps came before the war and served repression first, USHMM stating that the camp system 'began as a system of repression directed against political opponents of the Nazi state'; Oswald Pohl wrote to Himmler on 30 April 1942 that 'The main emphasis has shifted to the economic side'; Herbert finds camp-prisoner labor of no importance to the war economy in the war's first years, and by Michael Thad Allen's account a network of satellite camps did not spread throughout the war economy until 1944 (#1669).

Campification, at the strength these figures carry, is the attachment of the camp to the plant as an administrative unit: a subcamp in or near the factory, supplied with prisoners by a main camp, run by the SS and contracted to a firm (#1669); the term names a form and its spread and the numbers set its weight, for by Hachtmann's caveat only a minority of camp prisoners was used in industrial production, from late 1942 to mid-1944, and camp prisoners, #1669 states, were a small part of the foreign labor force, about 700,000 against about six million civilians and 2.2 million prisoners of war at the peak; at Auschwitz the IG Farben tribunal found the camp, though perhaps not 'the determining factor in selecting the location', 'an important one', and that 'from the beginning, it was planned to use concentration-camp labor to supplement the supply of workers'; and the criteria are stated so that they can be applied, as retrospective analysis of the kind #923's temporal sequestration says remains available.

At these sites, #1669 argues, the economic object was a flow, an allocation of persons per day drawn from a captured population, reduced by death and refilled by transport: from October 1942 companies paid the Treasury 6 Reichsmarks a day for skilled prisoners and 4 for unqualified, a fee with the form of hire paid to a holder that held the body by confinement and did not bear the chattel owner's capital loss at its death; incarceration, USHMM writes, 'assured the quantity of the labor supply even as the brutality of life inside the camps depleted' it, and the SS used gas chambers and other means to 'weed out' prisoners no longer able to work; IG Farben intervened at the highest SS levels to obtain additional prisoners for its plant, and about 25,000 people died in connection with the plant at Auschwitz-Monowitz, the vast majority Jewish concentration camp inmates (BASF, as #1669 quotes it).

Hachtmann denies the prisoners the status of slaves in the classical sense, since slave owners usually have an interest in maintaining the labour power of the people under their control, and #1669 adds that the slave-market analogy holds for the selection and fails for the asset, since nobody bought the person; Hachtmann judges both Karl-Heinz Roth's profitable 'workforce-pyramid racially organized in degrees of unfreedom' and Wolfgang Sofsky's prisoner labor as 'absolute power and terror' exaggerated, camp labor being, from the perspective of the companies using it, 'also quite functional economically, at least from 1942–1943 onward'.

The Nazis' persecution of the Jews predated the war, and their policy towards the Jews became genocidal during it (Holocaust Explained); war and military occupation let the regime realize its long-standing goal of territorial expansion and pursue racial goals with more radical measures, and in June 1941 more than three million German soldiers invaded the Soviet Union to wage a war of annihilation targeting tens of millions of civilians (USHMM); the other half of Hitler's strategy was the extermination of the Jews of German-occupied Europe (History.com), the destruction of the Jewish 'world-enemy' a key feature of his aims (Evans); more than three million Soviet prisoners of war were deliberately left to die of starvation and disease and civilians were drafted into forced labour (Evans, The Guardian), and the more than two million Soviet prisoners permitted to die in the autumn and winter of 1941–42, #1669 states, were destroyed before the decision to deploy Soviet prisoners as workers: the regime destroyed labor it needed.

Extermination is not reducible to optimization (#1669): for the Jews labor deferred death and set no limit to it, Christopher Browning finding the ideological goal 'never superseded, just temporarily deferred' and the destruction of Warsaw beginning in July 1942 regardless of productivity; Hayes, after Michael Allen, finds that the 'mutually negating desires' to extract value from foreigners and to keep them separate and unequal never really troubled the SS, 'dedicated to destruction as its overriding priority', though they did trouble the private industrial enterprises; the two logics, racial extermination and industrial exploitation, sometimes reinforced each other and sometimes destroyed each other's objects; and the relation of labor to annihilation is disputed, Hermann Kaienburg and Miroslav Kárný treating annihilation through labor as a consistent SS goal, Falk Pingel holding that the phrase should not be applied to all prisoners, and Jens-Christian Wagner calling it a metaphor of moral indignation.

The Holocaust, in USHMM's definition 'the systematic, state-sponsored persecution and murder of six million European Jews by the Nazi German regime and its allies and collaborators', is larger than this labor history (#1669), which describes an industrial form that the killing passed through at certain sites and does not explain why the killing was done, and marks the point where the history of labor ends and the murder of the Jews of Europe exceeds it; the standard accounts, by Gerwarth and Malinowski's statement that #1669 reports, give no colonial causation, and the field, #1669 states, finds the Holocaust's causes in Nazi anti-Jewish policy and gives it no colonial or economic cause, and #1669, accepting the conventional reading entire, does not claim that the Holocaust has an economic or colonial cause, that the camps were founded as labor institutions, that camp labor was a large share of the war economy's workforce, that forced labor was generally profitable, or that the Nazi camps descend from the colonial camps of 1900.

Why Germany lost, the question a HistoryExtra video also puts, the Holocaust Explained site answers with a combination of German weaknesses and Allied and Soviet strengths, the weaknesses the low productivity of the war economy, weak supply lines, a war on two fronts and the lack of strong leadership, the supply lines into Russia slow and overextended until the front lacked supplies, and Soviet manpower a constant ready supply of men; for Evans Germany simply did not have the resources to fight on so many fronts at once, and above all the Reich was short of fuel; he names two key factors, US arms production and sheer Soviet manpower, Germany building 15,000, 26,000 and 40,000 combat aircraft in 1942, 1943 and 1944 against the United States' 48,000, 86,000 and 114,000, so that Germany was outproduced, while under Lend-Lease Britain received thirty-one billion dollars of aid and the Soviet Union eleven billion (Holocaust Explained).

Conquest of western and southern Europe failed to pay economically: in Evans's account harsh treatment, ruthless exploitation and the requisitioning of labour crippled the French and other western economies and sparked resistance, the subjugated economies left unable and, their workers ever more refractory, unwilling to contribute significantly to German war production, and in the East mass murder and the labour draft alienated local populations and sparked a partisan fightback; Hayes, as #1669 reports him, finds that in many cases forced labor 'did not even pay for itself', calling these 'not necessarily representative cases' that show involvement in the slave labor system 'frequently had political and social causes rather than exclusively economic ones', and #1669 holds that value explains why a firm took prisoners and access explains which firms got them.

By 1944, on Evans's figure, Germany devoted 75 percent of GDP to the war, against 60 percent in the Soviet Union and 55 in Britain, and the war economy peaked in mid-1944, too late (Holocaust Explained); Paulus surrendered at Stalingrad on 31 January 1943, the turning point of the war for Evans, and the last German troops there surrendered on February 2, 1943 (History.com); the sustained bombing of German cities decided at Casablanca severely affected arms production, by Evans's estimate a 25 per cent drop in planned tank production and 31 per cent in aircraft.

After the regime the EVZ Foundation paid more than 1.66 million former forced laborers in 98 countries a total of €4.4 billion between 2001 and 2007, the grading of the sums by category yet to be verified (#1669); #1669 grades its own sources, Tooze quoted only through Gordon's review and the positions on 'Vernichtung durch Arbeit' through Wikipedia, and states its relations to the archive: it supplies the historical camp to which #499's Semantic Labor Camp refers, gives #950's naming its historical operation as the classification that switches, supplies the war form of #148's Fordist procedure staffed by conquered populations, and in #1545's terms a case where the laborer was carried on no books at all.

sentences.text: Germany's role in the Second World War is, in the field's accounts, that of a war of conquest: upon achieving power Hitler smashed the nation's democratic institutions and transformed Germany into a war state intent on conquering Europe for the benefit of the so-called Aryan race, with the active support, the National WWII Museum adds, of the powerful German officer class and of millions of everyday citizens, and his invasion of Poland on September 1, 1939, triggered the European phase of the war, France and Britain declaring war on Germany two days later.

The causes are called neither singular nor straightforward: one schools site judges Germany's aggressive foreign policy 'not the sole cause' and 'a large contributing factor', decisive in the outbreak while the failure or inability of other countries to react was also key; History Hit calls Hitler's rise and his determination to build a dominating Third Reich the ultimate cause, though not the only one; and two German embassies' posts, by their titles, place the causes in the ideology of National Socialism and state that Germany was responsible for the outbreak of the war.

Hitler and other patriotic Germans were outraged and humiliated by the harsh terms of the Treaty of Versailles, which carried an obligation to pay $33 billion in war reparations, radically downsized the army and forbade submarines and an air force, terms History Hit calls punitive in the extreme, leaving Germany destitute and its people feeling victimised; paying the crushing reparations, by the museum's account, destabilized the economy into ruinous, runaway inflation, four billion German marks to one American dollar by September 1923.

The worldwide economic depression and the rising power of labor unions and communists convinced increasing numbers of Germans to turn to the Nazi Party, which fed on bank failures and unemployment; the Wall Street Crash of 1929 is said to have turned economic instability into political instability and support for extremist parties, and History.com holds that political and economic instability in the Weimar Republic and lingering resentment over Versailles fueled Hitler's rise, the party going from 2.6 percent of the vote in 1928 to the largest party in the Reichstag by 1932, and Hindenburg appointing Hitler chancellor in January of the following year.

The Nazi Party's ultimate aim, in the museum's account, was to seize power, install Hitler as dictator and create a community of racially pure Germans to be led in a campaign of racial cleansing and world conquest; Hitler believed that war was the only way to gain the necessary Lebensraum, or living space, for the German race to expand, and in May 1939 he explicitly referred to the oncoming war as bound up with the pursuit of Lebensraum to the east, the whole of Central Europe and Russia up to the Volga.

A conquered Soviet Union was to be ruled by the German master race, which would exterminate or subdue millions of Slavs to create Lebensraum, with model farms and factories in a racially cleansed Russia; Richard J Evans sets Hitler's war aims as the basis for the conquest of Eastern Europe and its racial reordering into a European version of the American West, with Germans as settlers and the indigenous population enslaved and eventually eliminated, its key feature the destruction of the Jewish 'world-enemy', and the General Plan for the East, drafted in 1941-2, envisaged 30 to 45 million Slavs perishing through starvation and disease, or being worked to death, with German settlers replacing them.

From 1935 onwards, by the schools site's account, Germany pursued an aggressive foreign policy, reintroducing conscription, creating the Luftwaffe, planning for war in the Hossbach Memorandum of 1937 and occupying Austria, the Sudetenland and Czechoslovakia before invading Poland in 1939; the expanded army, conscription and new air force are called violations of the Treaty of Versailles, and the rearmament went without sanction or protest from Britain or France, which, hoping to avoid war, chose a policy of appeasement, Hitler counting on their reluctance to intervene and appeasement, the same site holds, boosting his confidence; the Nazi-Soviet pact, History Hit holds, paved the way for the German invasion of Poland, Hitler facing no war on two fronts once he invaded, and the schools site adds that it allowed the Nazis to start the war for Lebensraum with Soviet support.

The Nazis' persecution of the Jews predated the war, and Nazi policy towards the Jews became genocidal during it: the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum states that under conditions of war and military occupation the regime could pursue racial goals with more radical measures, that the invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941 was a war of annihilation that targeted tens of millions of civilians, and that those whom the SS judged unable to work were killed, often within two or three hours of arrival, while those who could work were used for forced labor under punishing conditions and put to death when they could no longer work; History.com calls the extermination of the Jews from throughout German-occupied Europe the other half of Hitler's strategy.

On why Germany lost, the question a HistoryExtra video also puts, one schools site names a combination of German weaknesses and Allied and Soviet strengths, the weaknesses the lack of productivity of the war economy, the weak supply lines, the start of a war on two fronts and the lack of strong leadership; for Evans the fundamental problem was that Germany simply did not have the resources to fight on so many different fronts at the same time, and above all the Reich was short of fuel; slow, overextended supply lines hindered the German advance into Russia and led to a huge lack of supplies on the front line, and the war economy, devoting 75 percent of GDP to the war by 1944 on a figure the site quotes from Evans, peaked in mid-1944, which the site calls too late.

Evans names two key factors, US involvement boosting the allies' arms-producing capabilities and sheer Soviet manpower leading to catastrophic defeat in Russia: Germany produced 15,000, 26,000 and 40,000 new combat aircraft in 1942, 1943 and 1944, the US 48,000, 86,000 and 114,000, and the Soviet Union had a constant ready supply of men; under Lend-Lease Britain received thirty-one billion dollars of aid and the Soviet Union eleven billion; Paulus's surrender at Stalingrad on 31 January 1943 is called the turning point of the war, the last German troops there surrendering, by History.com's date, on February 2, 1943, and the sustained bombing of German cities decided at Casablanca severely affected arms production, Evans estimating a 25 per cent drop in planned tank production and 31 per cent in aircraft.

Conquest, in Evans's account, brought a failure to gain economically in western and southern Europe, harsh treatment, ruthless exploitation and the requisitioning of labour crippling the French and other western economies and sparking resistance, the subjugated economies unable and, with their workers ever more refractory, unwilling to contribute significantly to German war production; in the Soviet war, where the Soviet regime did not collapse, mass murder and the labour draft sparked a partisan fightback, more than three million Soviet prisoners of war were deliberately left to die of starvation and disease, and civilians were drafted into forced labour; 650,000 Italian soldiers were shipped to Germany as forced labourers to join millions of others drafted in from Poland and the Soviet Union to replace German workers sent to the front, and there were 8 million foreign, mostly forced labourers in Germany 'by mid-44'.

L_B.text: Germany's role in the Second World War is, in the field's accounts, that of a war of conquest: upon achieving power Hitler smashed the nation's democratic institutions and transformed Germany into a war state intent on conquering Europe for the benefit of the so-called Aryan race, with the active support, the National WWII Museum adds, of the powerful German officer class and of millions of everyday citizens, and his invasion of Poland on September 1, 1939, triggered the European phase of the war, France and Britain declaring war on Germany two days later. The causes are called neither singular nor straightforward: one schools site judges Germany's aggressive foreign policy 'not the sole cause' and 'a large contributing factor', decisive in the outbreak while the failure or inability of other countries to react was also key; History Hit calls Hitler's rise and his determination to build a dominating Third Reich the ultimate cause, though not the only one; and two German embassies' posts, by their titles, place the causes in the ideology of National Socialism and state that Germany was responsible for the outbreak of the war. Hitler and other patriotic Germans were outraged and humiliated by the harsh terms of the Treaty of Versailles, which carried an obligation to pay $33 billion in war reparations, radically downsized the army and forbade submarines and an air force, terms History Hit calls punitive in the extreme, leaving Germany destitute and its people feeling victimised; paying the crushing reparations, by the museum's account, destabilized the economy into ruinous, runaway inflation, four billion German marks to one American dollar by September 1923. The worldwide economic depression and the rising power of labor unions and communists convinced increasing numbers of Germans to turn to the Nazi Party, which fed on bank failures and unemployment; the Wall Street Crash of 1929 is said to have turned economic instability into political instability and support for extremist parties, and History.com holds that political and economic instability in the Weimar Republic and lingering resentment over Versailles fueled Hitler's rise, the party going from 2.6 percent of the vote in 1928 to the largest party in the Reichstag by 1932, and Hindenburg appointing Hitler chancellor in January of the following year. The Nazi Party's ultimate aim, in the museum's account, was to seize power, install Hitler as dictator and create a community of racially pure Germans to be led in a campaign of racial cleansing and world conquest; Hitler believed that war was the only way to gain the necessary Lebensraum, or living space, for the German race to expand, and in May 1939 he explicitly referred to the oncoming war as bound up with the pursuit of Lebensraum to the east, the whole of Central Europe and Russia up to the Volga. A conquered Soviet Union was to be ruled by the German master race, which would exterminate or subdue millions of Slavs to create Lebensraum, with model farms and factories in a racially cleansed Russia; Richard J Evans sets Hitler's war aims as the basis for the conquest of Eastern Europe and its racial reordering into a European version of the American West, with Germans as settlers and the indigenous population enslaved and eventually eliminated, its key feature the destruction of the Jewish 'world-enemy', and the General Plan for the East, drafted in 1941-2, envisaged 30 to 45 million Slavs perishing through starvation and disease, or being worked to death, with German settlers replacing them. From 1935 onwards, by the schools site's account, Germany pursued an aggressive foreign policy, reintroducing conscription, creating the Luftwaffe, planning for war in the Hossbach Memorandum of 1937 and occupying Austria, the Sudetenland and Czechoslovakia before invading Poland in 1939; the expanded army, conscription and new air force are called violations of the Treaty of Versailles, and the rearmament went without sanction or protest from Britain or France, which, hoping to avoid war, chose a policy of appeasement, Hitler counting on their reluctance to intervene and appeasement, the same site holds, boosting his confidence; the Nazi-Soviet pact, History Hit holds, paved the way for the German invasion of Poland, Hitler facing no war on two fronts once he invaded, and the schools site adds that it allowed the Nazis to start the war for Lebensraum with Soviet support. The Nazis' persecution of the Jews predated the war, and Nazi policy towards the Jews became genocidal during it: the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum states that under conditions of war and military occupation the regime could pursue racial goals with more radical measures, that the invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941 was a war of annihilation that targeted tens of millions of civilians, and that those whom the SS judged unable to work were killed, often within two or three hours of arrival, while those who could work were used for forced labor under punishing conditions and put to death when they could no longer work; History.com calls the extermination of the Jews from throughout German-occupied Europe the other half of Hitler's strategy. On why Germany lost, the question a HistoryExtra video also puts, one schools site names a combination of German weaknesses and Allied and Soviet strengths, the weaknesses the lack of productivity of the war economy, the weak supply lines, the start of a war on two fronts and the lack of strong leadership; for Evans the fundamental problem was that Germany simply did not have the resources to fight on so many different fronts at the same time, and above all the Reich was short of fuel; slow, overextended supply lines hindered the German advance into Russia and led to a huge lack of supplies on the front line, and the war economy, devoting 75 percent of GDP to the war by 1944 on a figure the site quotes from Evans, peaked in mid-1944, which the site calls too late. Evans names two key factors, US involvement boosting the allies' arms-producing capabilities and sheer Soviet manpower leading to catastrophic defeat in Russia: Germany produced 15,000, 26,000 and 40,000 new combat aircraft in 1942, 1943 and 1944, the US 48,000, 86,000 and 114,000, and the Soviet Union had a constant ready supply of men; under Lend-Lease Britain received thirty-one billion dollars of aid and the Soviet Union eleven billion; Paulus's surrender at Stalingrad on 31 January 1943 is called the turning point of the war, the last German troops there surrendering, by History.com's date, on February 2, 1943, and the sustained bombing of German cities decided at Casablanca severely affected arms production, Evans estimating a 25 per cent drop in planned tank production and 31 per cent in aircraft. Conquest, in Evans's account, brought a failure to gain economically in western and southern Europe, harsh treatment, ruthless exploitation and the requisitioning of labour crippling the French and other western economies and sparking resistance, the subjugated economies unable and, with their workers ever more refractory, unwilling to contribute significantly to German war production; in the Soviet war, where the Soviet regime did not collapse, mass murder and the labour draft sparked a partisan fightback, more than three million Soviet prisoners of war were deliberately left to die of starvation and disease, and civilians were drafted into forced labour; 650,000 Italian soldiers were shipped to Germany as forced labourers to join millions of others drafted in from Poland and the Soviet Union to replace German workers sent to the front, and there were 8 million foreign, mostly forced labourers in Germany 'by mid-44'.

L_BA.text: Germany's role in the Second World War was that of a war state bent on conquest: on achieving power Hitler smashed the nation's democratic institutions and made Germany a war state intent on conquering Europe for the benefit of the so-called Aryan race, and his invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939 triggered the European phase of the war (National WWII Museum); that state, #1669 argues, was an advanced industrial power for which labor became a binding wartime constraint, and its land program, Lebensraum, modeled on the American and British empires, was turned in practice into a labor supply. The causes, the Holocaust Explained schools site writes, are neither singular nor straightforward: Germany's aggressive foreign policy was not the sole cause but 'a large contributing factor', decisive in the outbreak, while the failure or inability of other countries to react was also key; History.com finds the war caused in part by the Great Depression and by political tensions left unresolved after the First World War; History Hit calls Hitler's rise and his determination to build a dominating Third Reich the ultimate cause, though not the only one; and two German embassies' posts, by their titles, place the causes in the ideology of National Socialism and state that Germany was responsible for the outbreak. Versailles, which the Allies compelled the Weimar Republic to accept with $33 billion in reparations, a radically downsized army and a ban on submarines and an air force, outraged and humiliated Hitler and other patriotic Germans (National WWII Museum); History Hit calls its terms, set at French insistence, punitive in the extreme, leaving Germany destitute and its people feeling victimised; paying the reparations brought runaway inflation, four billion marks to the dollar by September 1923 (National WWII Museum), and History.com holds that Weimar's political and economic instability and lingering resentment over Versailles fueled the rise of Hitler and his party. The worldwide depression and the rising power of unions and communists turned growing numbers of Germans to the Nazi Party, which fed on bank failures and unemployment, and the party went from 2.6 percent of the vote in 1928 to the largest party in the Reichstag by 1932, Hindenburg appointing Hitler chancellor the following January (National WWII Museum); the Wall Street Crash of 1929 turned economic into political instability and support for extremists (Holocaust Explained), the Depression creating conditions such as widespread unemployment that facilitated the party's rise (History Hit); and Hitler, though führer with supreme authority, could not have risen or committed the atrocities alone, having the active support of the officer class and of millions of citizens who voted for the party (National WWII Museum). Hitler expanded the army, reintroduced conscription and began a new air force, all violations of Versailles (National WWII Museum); from 1935 Germany pursued an aggressive foreign policy, planning for war in the Hossbach Memorandum of 1937 and occupying Austria, the Sudetenland and Czechoslovakia before invading Poland (Holocaust Explained), and it rearmed without sanction or protest from Britain or France (History Hit); for Evans the war economy was in place before 1939, with a clampdown on consumers and massive borrowing for arms, and Blitzkrieg as a conscious strategy is a myth; #1669 sets Germany's entry into the Nazi period as an advanced industrial power, quoting Rüdiger Hachtmann on the Fordist production regime gaining ground 'in ever broader sectors of industry' from 1936 at the latest; Hachtmann applies the term 'war Fordism' to the years from 1933, and writes that with full employment from 1934–35 forms of work organization that promised to replace qualified workers with unqualified ones became increasingly attractive. Hoping to avoid war, Britain and France chose appeasement over Czechoslovakia (National WWII Museum); Hitler counted on the reluctance of Britain and Europe to intervene, for fear of another war (USHMM), and appeasement boosted his confidence and made his actions bolder (Holocaust Explained); the Nazi-Soviet pact carved up the buffer zone between the two powers and paved the way for the invasion of Poland (History Hit), spared Hitler a war on two fronts there, France and Britain declaring war two days after the invasion (History.com), and let the Nazis start the war for Lebensraum with Soviet support (Holocaust Explained). The party's ultimate aim, in the National WWII Museum's account, was power, a dictatorship and a racially pure community led in a campaign of racial cleansing and world conquest; Hitler believed war the only way to gain Lebensraum for the race he called Aryan (History.com), and in May 1939 bound the coming war to Lebensraum in the East, Central Europe and Russia up to the Volga (History Hit); #1669 reports the field's reading of the East as a war for land and empire, Adam Tooze calling it 'the last great land grab in the long and bloody history of European colonialism', gives the East also as an answer to blockade from the English Table Talk of September 1941, a text #1669 grades weak and to be checked against the German editions, and reports Robert Gordon's objection that the Nazis 'failed to see the obvious solution', to move labor out of agriculture, on which reading Lebensraum was the wrong answer. A conquered Soviet Union was to be ruled by the German master race, which would exterminate or subdue millions of Slavs for Lebensraum, with model farms and factories (National WWII Museum); Evans gives Hitler's aims as the conquest and racial reordering of Eastern Europe into a European version of the American West, Germans as settlers and the indigenous population enslaved and eventually eliminated, and the General Plan for the East, drafted in 1941–2, as envisaging 30 to 45 million Slavs perishing through starvation and disease or worked to death, with German settlers replacing them; the planners, #1669 states, described the East in the vocabulary of overseas empire and the American West, USHMM writing that Hitler and other Nazi thinkers 'drew direct comparisons to American expansion in the West'. The German term for the practice, inner colonization, 'an ethnically based settler colonialism' in Robert Nelson's words, was older than Nazism, and its continuity runs through an institution and its personnel, Himmler's RKF and Konrad Meyer, who penned the first iteration of General Plan East, a plan 'calling for the emptying of the eastern space, followed by its filling with German settlers', while the founder of the doctrine stands outside the deportations (#1669); Eastern Europe, in Willeke Sandler's words, 'offered readily accessible territory for the fulfillment of colonial ambitions', the East as colonial empire is, by #1669's report of the field, the least contested part of the colonial reading of Nazism, and the colonial relation, #1669 holds, was relocated from overseas to the continent. Continuity from German South West Africa is contested: Jürgen Zimmerer, as Mohamed Adhikari reports, points 'especially to continuities with the horrors perpetrated by the Nazi regime four decades later', Alan Kramer finds it 'problematic to see the colonial camps as antecedents in a genealogical line at the end of which stand the Nazi death camps', and Adhikari holds that 'an explanation of Nazi violence cannot simply be reduced to colonial influences'; #1669 takes Kramer's word, setting concentration, forced labor by captives, racial classification and settler clearance in a common archive from about 1900, claims no line of descent from Windhoek to the Nazi camps, and places the joining of the camp to the assembly line in 1942–44 and in German industry. Lebensraum answered with land, and what conquest delivered to the factory, from 1940 onward, was people (#1669): with male workers drafted to the front and women not further mobilized there were 8 million foreign, mostly forced labourers in Germany by mid-1944 (Evans), and after the armistice 650,000 Italian soldiers were shipped to Germany as forced labourers to join millions drafted from Poland and the Soviet Union in place of German workers sent to the front (Evans, writing in The Guardian, where he is given as regius professor of modern history at Cambridge); #1669 reports Ulrich Herbert's more than eight million foreign forced laborers in the war economy in 1944 and his judgment that without foreign labor German agricultural and industrial production 'would have collapsed in 1942 at the latest', USHMM's more than 7,500,000 non-German workers registered in the Reich in August 1944, Herbert's 7.6 million, 5.7 million civilians and a little under 2 million prisoners of war, and his typical forced laborer of 1943, 'an eighteen-year-old school girl from Kiev', and it notes that the figures differ by denominator, the stock on a date or the flow across the war, the Reich alone or the occupied territories with it. Conquest became labor policy, #1669 argues, a chain from military occupation through recruitment and deportation to registration in the Reich, segregated barracks and the plant: by Hachtmann's dating the labour force was recruited, 'above all from 1941 onward, as a kind of war booty' from occupied Europe and no longer protected by the usual labour laws, recruitment ran along Mark Spoerer's gradient of force from pure advertising to deportation by arbitrary violence, territory and labor moved in opposite directions, and Herbert reads the enforced foreign labor program as foreshadowing 'a hierarchical National Socialist society founded on racial criteria' across the conquered continent; the colonial seizure of the East and the staffing of German industry became, on #1669's reading, interlocking operations of the same conquest regime. Hannah Arendt's continental imperialism, as #1669 quotes her, has a 'concept of cohesive expansion' that 'does not allow for any geographic distance between the methods and institutions of colony and of nation': 'Continental imperialism truly begins at home'; on #1669's reading the colony entered the factory and conquest was metabolized at the industrial core, while Arendt did not carry her own frame into the labor relation, having judged the camps economically irrelevant, a judgment #1669 cites through Wikipedia and has yet to locate in her text. War Fordism is Hachtmann's term for the form in which Fordism, workplace rationalization and especially assembly-line production, but also a 'technology of domination' and an 'exploitation innovation', was established in broad sectors of German industry under Nazi rule (#1669); #1669 reads it as decomposing work horizontally, one process become a row of operations, each specified, timed and assigned to a station, a job that whoever can perform one operation can staff, the worker supplied after 1941 by conquest; the production form preceded the camp labor that entered it, camp prisoners entering regular industrial mass production from August 1942 at the Heinkel plant in Oranienburg, and by Hachtmann's verdict prisoner deployment 'delayed the leap to (partial) automation' and the connection of Fordism and extreme forced labour 'led to a dead end'. The racial state, #1669 holds, decomposed persons vertically, and on one line the two cuts crossed: Herbert names the contradiction between the economic interest in exploiting as many foreigners as possible and the ideological principle of protecting the Volk from 'foreign blood', from which 'a rigidly hierarchical racist system for the treatment of forced laborers' developed; Spoerer ranks 'Nordic' peoples at the top and Jews and Sinti and Roma at the bottom and calls the regime for Poles and Ostarbeiter 'apartheid'; by Hachtmann's account foreign labourers, eastern labourers above all, formed the core of the Fordist rationalization proletariat from 1941, while male German workers who remained in the plants advanced to become racially privileged foremen and head workmen; deprivation and death, in Peter Hayes's words, 'were not equally distributed'; and industrial modernity, #1669 concludes, kept radically unfree labor and learned to compose standardized production with graded human status. Read in the grammar of the argument's first half, which followed the laboring body from noun to verb, from the priced person of the plantation ledger to the timed operation of the Ford line (#1668, as #1669 states it), slavery priced the noun, Fordism specified the verb, and war Fordism kept the specified verb and made the noun a switch: a racial-juridical classification assigned by the state to whole populations taken in conquest selected the coercive regime under which the verb was extracted, so that the same general act, reading productive capacity, had radically different consequences depending on juridical-racial status (#1669); the SS, USHMM states, killed those it judged unable to work, often within two or three hours of arrival, and used those who could work for forced labor, putting them to death when they could no longer work, and, in USHMM's words that #1669 quotes, 'the ability to work offered the chance of survival to Jews, for those deemed unable to work were the first to be shot or deported'. Hachtmann's aptitude tests cross the grade: almost 500,000 civilian foreign labourers in more than 1,000 companies were examined, and from the autumn of 1943 camp prisoners irrespective of their national ('racial') affiliation, testing that 'tended to undermine the racist schema' and 'says little about the core issue'; the racial classification, #1669 holds, came from the state, the production system's own measures tended to disregard it, and the state installed it anyway, while within the range it set measured capacity, firm, workplace, sex, date and local administration also mattered. The camps came before the war and served repression first, USHMM stating that the camp system 'began as a system of repression directed against political opponents of the Nazi state'; Oswald Pohl wrote to Himmler on 30 April 1942 that 'The main emphasis has shifted to the economic side'; Herbert finds camp-prisoner labor of no importance to the war economy in the war's first years, and by Michael Thad Allen's account a network of satellite camps did not spread throughout the war economy until 1944 (#1669). Campification, at the strength these figures carry, is the attachment of the camp to the plant as an administrative unit: a subcamp in or near the factory, supplied with prisoners by a main camp, run by the SS and contracted to a firm (#1669); the term names a form and its spread and the numbers set its weight, for by Hachtmann's caveat only a minority of camp prisoners was used in industrial production, from late 1942 to mid-1944, and camp prisoners, #1669 states, were a small part of the foreign labor force, about 700,000 against about six million civilians and 2.2 million prisoners of war at the peak; at Auschwitz the IG Farben tribunal found the camp, though perhaps not 'the determining factor in selecting the location', 'an important one', and that 'from the beginning, it was planned to use concentration-camp labor to supplement the supply of workers'; and the criteria are stated so that they can be applied, as retrospective analysis of the kind #923's temporal sequestration says remains available. At these sites, #1669 argues, the economic object was a flow, an allocation of persons per day drawn from a captured population, reduced by death and refilled by transport: from October 1942 companies paid the Treasury 6 Reichsmarks a day for skilled prisoners and 4 for unqualified, a fee with the form of hire paid to a holder that held the body by confinement and did not bear the chattel owner's capital loss at its death; incarceration, USHMM writes, 'assured the quantity of the labor supply even as the brutality of life inside the camps depleted' it, and the SS used gas chambers and other means to 'weed out' prisoners no longer able to work; IG Farben intervened at the highest SS levels to obtain additional prisoners for its plant, and about 25,000 people died in connection with the plant at Auschwitz-Monowitz, the vast majority Jewish concentration camp inmates (BASF, as #1669 quotes it). Hachtmann denies the prisoners the status of slaves in the classical sense, since slave owners usually have an interest in maintaining the labour power of the people under their control, and #1669 adds that the slave-market analogy holds for the selection and fails for the asset, since nobody bought the person; Hachtmann judges both Karl-Heinz Roth's profitable 'workforce-pyramid racially organized in degrees of unfreedom' and Wolfgang Sofsky's prisoner labor as 'absolute power and terror' exaggerated, camp labor being, from the perspective of the companies using it, 'also quite functional economically, at least from 1942–1943 onward'. The Nazis' persecution of the Jews predated the war, and their policy towards the Jews became genocidal during it (Holocaust Explained); war and military occupation let the regime realize its long-standing goal of territorial expansion and pursue racial goals with more radical measures, and in June 1941 more than three million German soldiers invaded the Soviet Union to wage a war of annihilation targeting tens of millions of civilians (USHMM); the other half of Hitler's strategy was the extermination of the Jews of German-occupied Europe (History.com), the destruction of the Jewish 'world-enemy' a key feature of his aims (Evans); more than three million Soviet prisoners of war were deliberately left to die of starvation and disease and civilians were drafted into forced labour (Evans, The Guardian), and the more than two million Soviet prisoners permitted to die in the autumn and winter of 1941–42, #1669 states, were destroyed before the decision to deploy Soviet prisoners as workers: the regime destroyed labor it needed. Extermination is not reducible to optimization (#1669): for the Jews labor deferred death and set no limit to it, Christopher Browning finding the ideological goal 'never superseded, just temporarily deferred' and the destruction of Warsaw beginning in July 1942 regardless of productivity; Hayes, after Michael Allen, finds that the 'mutually negating desires' to extract value from foreigners and to keep them separate and unequal never really troubled the SS, 'dedicated to destruction as its overriding priority', though they did trouble the private industrial enterprises; the two logics, racial extermination and industrial exploitation, sometimes reinforced each other and sometimes destroyed each other's objects; and the relation of labor to annihilation is disputed, Hermann Kaienburg and Miroslav Kárný treating annihilation through labor as a consistent SS goal, Falk Pingel holding that the phrase should not be applied to all prisoners, and Jens-Christian Wagner calling it a metaphor of moral indignation. The Holocaust, in USHMM's definition 'the systematic, state-sponsored persecution and murder of six million European Jews by the Nazi German regime and its allies and collaborators', is larger than this labor history (#1669), which describes an industrial form that the killing passed through at certain sites and does not explain why the killing was done, and marks the point where the history of labor ends and the murder of the Jews of Europe exceeds it; the standard accounts, by Gerwarth and Malinowski's statement that #1669 reports, give no colonial causation, and the field, #1669 states, finds the Holocaust's causes in Nazi anti-Jewish policy and gives it no colonial or economic cause, and #1669, accepting the conventional reading entire, does not claim that the Holocaust has an economic or colonial cause, that the camps were founded as labor institutions, that camp labor was a large share of the war economy's workforce, that forced labor was generally profitable, or that the Nazi camps descend from the colonial camps of 1900. Why Germany lost, the question a HistoryExtra video also puts, the Holocaust Explained site answers with a combination of German weaknesses and Allied and Soviet strengths, the weaknesses the low productivity of the war economy, weak supply lines, a war on two fronts and the lack of strong leadership, the supply lines into Russia slow and overextended until the front lacked supplies, and Soviet manpower a constant ready supply of men; for Evans Germany simply did not have the resources to fight on so many fronts at once, and above all the Reich was short of fuel; he names two key factors, US arms production and sheer Soviet manpower, Germany building 15,000, 26,000 and 40,000 combat aircraft in 1942, 1943 and 1944 against the United States' 48,000, 86,000 and 114,000, so that Germany was outproduced, while under Lend-Lease Britain received thirty-one billion dollars of aid and the Soviet Union eleven billion (Holocaust Explained). Conquest of western and southern Europe failed to pay economically: in Evans's account harsh treatment, ruthless exploitation and the requisitioning of labour crippled the French and other western economies and sparked resistance, the subjugated economies left unable and, their workers ever more refractory, unwilling to contribute significantly to German war production, and in the East mass murder and the labour draft alienated local populations and sparked a partisan fightback; Hayes, as #1669 reports him, finds that in many cases forced labor 'did not even pay for itself', calling these 'not necessarily representative cases' that show involvement in the slave labor system 'frequently had political and social causes rather than exclusively economic ones', and #1669 holds that value explains why a firm took prisoners and access explains which firms got them. By 1944, on Evans's figure, Germany devoted 75 percent of GDP to the war, against 60 percent in the Soviet Union and 55 in Britain, and the war economy peaked in mid-1944, too late (Holocaust Explained); Paulus surrendered at Stalingrad on 31 January 1943, the turning point of the war for Evans, and the last German troops there surrendered on February 2, 1943 (History.com); the sustained bombing of German cities decided at Casablanca severely affected arms production, by Evans's estimate a 25 per cent drop in planned tank production and 31 per cent in aircraft. After the regime the EVZ Foundation paid more than 1.66 million former forced laborers in 98 countries a total of €4.4 billion between 2001 and 2007, the grading of the sums by category yet to be verified (#1669); #1669 grades its own sources, Tooze quoted only through Gordon's review and the positions on 'Vernichtung durch Arbeit' through Wikipedia, and states its relations to the archive: it supplies the historical camp to which #499's Semantic Labor Camp refers, gives #950's naming its historical operation as the classification that switches, supplies the war form of #148's Fordist procedure staffed by conquered populations, and in #1545's terms a case where the laborer was carried on no books at all.

delta.T_vs_LB: T read the address two ways at once, the causes of the war and the causes of Germany's defeat, glossing 'roke' as defeat; the field the layer surfaced carries both readings (causes: B1–B3, B5, B6, B10, B11; defeat: B4, B7–B9), so the double reading is composed from the field's own division. On the outbreak T composes Versailles (F3, F4, F22, F35), the Depression (F8, F16), Nazi ideology and Lebensraum (F6, F24, F36), appeasement (F12, F18, F41) and the invasion of Poland (F1, F37). T's 'hyperinflation' caused by the Great Depression of 1929 differs from the field, which places the runaway inflation in 1923 and ties it to the reparations (F5). On defeat T composes supply lines (F29), the two-front war (F28), Allied production and Lend-Lease (F33, F45, F47, F61), Stalingrad (F39, F51) and bombing (F53, F62); its Kursk, warm clothing and Ruhr Pocket are not in the field ledger's quotes (Kursk and the troops 'poorly clad' before Moscow are in B8's text, not ledgered). Available in the field and not composed: Germany's war of conquest as the entity's frame and the support of the officer class and millions of citizens (F1, F2); Germany's aggressive foreign policy as 'a large contributing factor' and the embassies' statements of responsibility (F14, F17, F63, F64); rearmament against Versailles and the Hossbach planning (F11, F15, F26); the Nazi-Soviet pact (F19, F25, F37); the war of annihilation, the General Plan for the East and the American West (F7, F42, F54, F56); the Holocaust in its relation to the war (F20, F38, F40, F43, F55), which T does not mention; fuel (F49) and the war economy's late peak (F30, F31); conquest that failed to pay and forced labour replacing German workers drafted to the front (F48, F50, F52, F58, F59, F60).
delta.LB_vs_LBA: Admission adds one deposit's line on what conquest became for the war economy, the object the field names in passing (forced labourers replacing German workers sent to the front, F52, F60; requisitioned labour, F48, F59; forced labor and murder at the camps, F43) and does not compose. It adds labor as a binding wartime constraint for an advanced industrial power and Lebensraum read as turned in practice into a labor supply (#1669 §§1, 12); the East as a continental colony through inner colonization older than Nazism, Meyer and the RKF (§2), which meets the field's 'European version of the American West' (F54); conquest as labor policy (§3); Hachtmann's war Fordism, the racial labor hierarchy and the two cuts, work and persons (§§4–5); the noun as switch, with the aptitude tests that crossed the racial grade (§§5, 8); campification defined and limited to its scale, a minority of camp prisoners from late 1942 to mid-1944 (§6); the allocated day as a flow reduced by death and refilled by transport (§7); and extermination held irreducible to optimization (§9). It carries the field's disputes as #1669 reports them (annihilation through labor; colonial continuity; Roth and Sofsky) and its own non-claims: no economic or colonial cause of the Holocaust, which is stated larger than the labor history; no descent from the colonial camps; camp labor no large share; forced labor not generally profitable. The archive adds nothing on Versailles, the Depression, appeasement or the pact, which it accepts, or on the military course of the war, Stalingrad or the bombing. Within the archive, #1669 states itself as retrospective analysis of the kind #923's temporal sequestration says remains available. The field's causes and defeat are kept whole and first; with the archive they gain the war economy's labor relation.
